levels.name: Short Vowels & CVC Words
levels.description: Start with short vowel sounds and three-letter words.

levels.name: Silent "e" and Long Vowels
levels.description: Hear how a final silent e changes a vowel sound.

levels.name: Double Consonants
levels.description: Practise words with two matching consonants together.

levels.name: Common Digraphs (sh, ch, th, wh, ph)
levels.description: Learn common pairs of letters and their sounds.

levels.name: Blends (bl, br, cl, cr, dr, fl, fr, tr)
levels.description: Listen for consonants that blend at the start of a word.

levels.name: Syllable Patterns (2 syllables, stress)
levels.description: Break useful words into two spoken parts.

levels.name: Complex Patterns (silent letters, irregulars)
levels.description: Practise silent letters and less predictable spellings.

levels.name: Dictation & Phrases
levels.description: Listen and spell useful phrases for everyday situations.

levels.name: Commonly Misspelled Words
levels.description: Build confidence with useful words that are often misspelled.

levels.name: Longer Words and Double Letters
levels.description: Notice repeated letters and unstressed syllables in longer words.

levels.name: Professional and Abstract Vocabulary
levels.description: Spell precise words used in work, decisions and formal communication.

levels.name: Advanced Phrases and Sentences
levels.description: Use careful spelling in practical phrases and complete sentences.

patterns.description: A consonant, a short vowel and a final consonant.
A final e is silent and often changes the earlier vowel sound.
Notice two matching consonant letters in the spelling.
The letters sh usually represent /ʃ/.
The letters ch often represent /tʃ/.
The letters th can represent /θ/ or /ð/.
In Standard Southern British English, wh usually represents /w/.
The letters ph commonly represent /f/.
Hear /b/ followed by /l/ at the start.
Hear /b/ followed by /r/ at the start.
Hear /k/ followed by /l/ at the start.
Hear the tr consonant blend at the start.
Hear /f/ followed by /l/ at the start.
Hear /f/ followed by /r/, as in free, fresh and from.
Hear two syllables and notice which is stressed.
Some written letters have no separate spoken sound.
Some common words need extra practice because their spelling is less predictable.
Listen to a useful phrase, including the spaces between words.
Notice the unstressed letters in endings such as -ary and related word families.
Count repeated consonants carefully in longer words; a doubled letter does not always mean a longer sound.
Weak syllables often contain a schwa /ə/. Listen, then check which vowel letters the spelling uses.
Learn useful exceptions and borrowed spellings through repeated listening and careful recall.
Build longer words from familiar roots and endings such as -tion, -ity and -al.
Spell useful formal phrases and sentences, including the spaces between words.
